source_text: Caeterum, de incendio mundi, aut improvisum ignem cadere, aut difficile non credere, vulgaris erroris est. Quis enim sapientium dubitat, quis ignorat, omnia quae orta sunt, occidere; quae facta sunt, interire? coelum quoque, cum omnibus quae coelo continentur, ita, ut coepisse, desinere? fontium dulcis aqua maria nutrire, in vim ignis abiturum? Stoicis constans opinio est quod, consumpto humore, mundus hic omnis ignescat; et Epicureis, de elementorum conflagratione et mundi ruina, eadem ipsa sententia est. Loquitur Plato partes orbis nunc inundare, dicit nunc alternis vicibus ardescere; et, quum ipsum mundum perpetuum et insolubilem diceret esse fabricatum, addit tamen ipsi artifici, Deo soli et solubilem et esse mortalem. Ita nihil mirum est, si ista moles ab eo quo exstructa est, destruatur. Animadvertis philosophos eadem disputare quae dicimus, non quod nos simus eorum vestigia subsecuti, sed quod illi, de divinis praedicationibus Prophetarum, umbram interpolatae veritatis imitati sint. Sic etiam conditionem renascendi, sapientium clariores, Pythagoras primus, et praecipuus Plato, corrupta et dimidiata fide, tradiderunt: nam, corporibus dissolutis, solas animas volunt et perpetuo manere, et in alia nova corpora saepius commeare. Addunt istis et illa ad retorquendam veritatem, in pecudes, aves, belluas, hominum animas redire. Non philosophi sane studio, sed mimico vitio digna ista sententia est. Sed ad propositum satis est etiam in hoc sapientes vestros, in aliquam modum nobiscum consonare. Caeterum, quis tam stultus aut brutus est ut audeat repugnare hominem a Deo, ut primum potuisse fingi, ita posse denuo reformari? nihil esse post obitum, et ante ortum nihil fuisse; sicut de nihilo nasci licuit, ita de nasci licere reparari? Porro difficilius est id quod non sit incipere, quam id quod fuerit iterare. Tu perire et Deo credis, si quid oculis nostris hebetibus subtrahitur? Corpus omne, sive arescit in pulverem, sive in humorem solvitur, vel in cinerem comprimitur, vel in nidorem tenuatur, subducitur nobis; sed Deo, elementorum custodia reservatur. Nec, ut creditis, ullum damnum sepulturae timemus, sed veterem et meliorem consuetudinem humandi frequentamus. Vide adeo quam, in solatium nostri, resurrectionem futuram omnis natura meditetur! Sol demergit et nascitur, astra labuntur et redeunt, flores occidunt et reviviscunt, post senium arbusta frondescunt, semina non nisi corrupta revirescunt: ita corpus in saeculo, ut arbores in hyberno, occultant virorem ariditate mentita. Quid festinas, ut cruda adhuc hyeme reviviscat et redeat? expectandum nobis etiam corporis ver est. Nec ignoro plerosque, conscientia meritorum, nihil se esse post mortem magis optare quam credere: malunt enim exstingui penitus, quam ad supplicia reparari. Quorum error augetur, et in saeculo libertate remissa, et Dei patientia maxima: cujus quanto judicium tardum, tanto magis justum est.
thought_title: Resurrection and the Nature of the World
pass_a_gloss: Moreover, about the conflagration of the world, or that fire falls unexpectedly, or it is difficult not to believe, it is a common error. For who of the wise men doubts, who is ignorant, that all things which have arisen will perish, and that which has been made will pass away? Also the heaven, with all things which the heaven contains, will cease just as it began. The sweet water of the springs will nourish the seas and will be consumed by the force of fire. The constant opinion of the Stoics is that, when the moisture is consumed, the whole world will ignite; and the Epicureans have the same opinion about the conflagration of the elements and the ruin of the world. Plato says that parts of the world now flood, now burn in turn; and when he said that the world itself is perpetual and indestructible, he adds that it is nonetheless soluble and mortal for the Creator, God alone. So it is not surprising if this mass is destroyed by the one by whom it was constructed. We notice that philosophers discuss the same things that we say, not because we have followed in their footsteps, but because they have imitated the shadow of interpolated truth from the divine predictions of the Prophets. Thus, the most renowned wise men, Pythagoras first and especially Plato, have also handed down the condition of rebirth, with corrupted and partial faith: for, with bodies dissolved, they want the souls alone to remain and to migrate frequently into new bodies. They add to these things also that which is used to twist the truth, that the souls of men return into beasts, birds, and animals. This opinion is not worthy of philosophical study, but of a mimetic vice. But it is enough for our purpose that your wise men also agree with us in some way. Moreover, who is so foolish or brutish as to dare to resist that man can be reformed by God, just as he was first able to be created? That there is nothing after death and nothing before birth; just as it was possible to be born from nothing, so it is possible to be repaired from birth. Furthermore, it is more difficult for that which does not exist to begin than for that which has been to be repeated. Do you believe that something perishes and is hidden from God, if it is withdrawn from our dull eyes? Every body, whether it withers into dust, or is dissolved into moisture, or is compressed into ash, or is thinned into a smell, is withdrawn from us; but for God, the custody of the elements is reserved. Nor do we fear, as you believe, any loss of burial, but we frequent the old and better custom of burying. See how all nature meditates the future resurrection for our consolation! The sun sets and is born, the stars fall and return, flowers die and revive, trees sprout leaves after old age, seeds do not revive unless they have been corrupted: so the body in the world, like trees in winter, hides its vigor with pretended dryness. Why do you hasten, that it may revive and return while the winter is still raw? We must also wait for the spring of the body. And I am not unaware that many, by the consciousness of their merits, desire nothing more after death than to believe: for they prefer to be extinguished completely rather than to be repaired for punishments. The error of these people is increased, both by the freedom of the world and by God's greatest patience: whose judgment is all the more just, the slower it is.

pass_b_english: The idea that the world will end in fire, or that flames will fall without warning, is a common mistake—indeed, it is hard not to believe it. After all, which wise person doubts, which one does not know, that everything born must die and everything made must pass away? Even the heavens, along with all they contain, will cease just as they began. The sweet water of the springs feeds the seas, only to be consumed by the force of fire. The Stoics hold a fixed opinion: once the moisture is gone, the whole world will ignite. The Epicureans share the very same view on the conflagration of the elements and the ruin of the world. Plato says that parts of the world now flood, now burn in turn; and although he called the world itself perpetual and indestructible, he added that it remains soluble and mortal for the Creator, God alone. So it is no surprise if this vast structure is destroyed by the one who built it.

You see that philosophers discuss the very same things we do, not because we followed in their footsteps, but because they imitated a shadow of distorted truth from the divine predictions of the Prophets. Thus the most renowned wise men—Pythagoras first, and especially Plato—also handed down the doctrine of rebirth, but with a corrupted and half‑hearted faith: they claim that once bodies dissolve, souls alone remain forever and migrate repeatedly into new bodies. They even add the twisting claim that human souls return into beasts, birds, and wild animals. Such an opinion deserves not philosophical study but a mimetic vice. Still, for our purpose it is enough that your own wise men agree with us in some measure.

Who is so foolish or brutish as to deny that God can reform a human being, just as He first created him? That nothing exists after death and nothing existed before birth; just as it was possible to be born from nothing, so it is possible to be restored from birth. Indeed, it is harder for what does not exist to begin than for what has existed to be repeated. Do you believe something perishes and is hidden from God simply because it is withdrawn from our dull eyes? Every body, whether it withers into dust, dissolves into moisture, compresses into ash, or thins into a scent, is taken from us; but for God the custody of the elements is reserved. Nor do we fear any loss from burial, as you suppose; we keep the old and better custom of interring the dead. Look how all nature meditates the future resurrection for our consolation! The sun sets and rises, the stars fall and return, flowers die and revive, trees sprout leaves after old age, seeds do not revive unless they have first corrupted: so the body in the world, like trees in winter, hides its vigor behind a pretended dryness. Why do you hurry, demanding it revive and return while winter is still raw? We must also wait for the body’s spring.

I am not unaware that many, by the consciousness of their merits, desire nothing more after death than to believe there is nothing; for they prefer to be extinguished completely rather than be restored for punishments. The error of these people is increased both by the world’s lax freedom and by God’s greatest patience: whose judgment is all the more just, the slower it is.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause translation, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that preserves all nuances, including the distinction between the philosophers' 'shadow of interpolated truth' (umbram interpolatae veritatis) and the author's own position. All theological distinctions regarding the nature of the soul, the resurrection, and the Creator are maintained. Scripture references are not present in the source text, so none are required in the translation.
